"Northern Territory police failed to act on a string of self-harm and suicide attempts in caged police vehicles before the death of a vulnerable 23-year-old man last year, a coroner has found. NT coroner Greg Cavanagh has criticised police for failing to act on an internal report recommending CCTV cameras be installed in caged vehicles in 2013, following an earlier death in custody. In the three years between the two deaths, there were at least 16 attempted suicides in caged vehicles. “In six cases the persons were not detected until they were semi-conscious or unconscious,” Cavanagh found. “It wasn’t a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when.”

On 16 September last year, two officers were making their way through Darwin, on their way to investigate a noise complaint, when they came across the scene of a serious crash. A Toyota Hilux had smashed into a palm tree on the corner of the Stuart Highway and Bargot Road, not far from Darwin airport. Hiding behind some vegetation was Dale Scott Walkinshaw, 23. Walkinshaw was unharmed but held his passenger in his arms. The young woman, whom he had met earlier at a bar, was in and out of consciousness, having suffered an injury to her back. Walkinshaw was well over the limit, returning a reading of 0.149.

The world had shrunk to the flashing red and blue lights painting the tropical foliage in ghastly, repetitive strokes. One moment he was holding the woman, whispering apologies she couldn't hear, the next he was being pulled to his feet, the cold click of handcuffs sealing his fate. He watched, helpless, as paramedics gently lifted her onto a stretcher. Her eyes fluttered open for a second, finding his, a flicker of fear and pain that would sear itself into his memory.

“Come on, mate. Let’s go,” one of the officers said, his voice not unkind but firm with procedure. They led him to the caged police vehicle, a white van that seemed to absorb all the light around it. The door to the rear compartment opened with a hollow scrape, revealing a small, stark metal box. As Dale was guided inside, the humid Darwin air was cut off by the final, echoing slam of the door.

Darkness. And the heat. It was immediate and oppressive. The only light was a thin sliver from the bottom of the door, the only view a distorted glimpse of passing streetlights through a small, thick-wired grille. From the front cabin, he could hear the muffled crackle of the radio and the low murmur of the officers’ voices. They were talking about the noise complaint they had been heading to, about the paperwork this crash would generate. Their world continued, oblivious.

In the cage, Dale’s world was ending. The alcohol was a poisoned fire in his veins, fuelling a frantic slideshow of his mistakes. The mangled Hilux. The woman’s limp body in his arms. The reading of 0.149. He saw a future of courtrooms, guilt, and the four walls of a prison cell. The metal box he was in felt like a coffin, a preview of the life he had just authored for himself. He pressed his face against the hot metal wall, the vibrations of the road a merciless rhythm counting down his wasted years. Panic, thick and suffocating, clawed at his throat. He was alone. Utterly and completely alone. The world outside was a million miles away, and no one could see him. No one was watching.

At the Darwin watch house, the van backed into the sally port with a series of loud beeps. The engine cut, and the sudden silence was profound. An officer walked to the rear, key in hand, the mundane end to a routine drunk-driving arrest. He turned the lock and pulled the heavy door open. For a moment, he simply stared into the dark interior. Then, a sharp, panicked shout. “Get a medic! Now!”

But it was too late. Dale Scott Walkinshaw had become the tragic fulfillment of the coroner’s prophecy. He was another number added to the list of the unseen, his final, desperate act unfolding in the unmonitored darkness of a metal box on wheels. The internal report from 2013 sat in a filing cabinet somewhere, its recommendations unheeded. For Dale, it was never a matter of if, but simply when. And his time had just run out."
